g3m-3-10-01-warm-1.text: Hoo, welcome to Chapter 10! Let's open our old book to a new time and place: Leipzig, Germany, about 300 years ago. Meet Johann Sebastian Bach. He wrote music, and in his music, one measure is one whole. Bach could fill a measure in many ways: one long note, or shorter notes that take the same time. Let's listen.

g3m-3-10-01-think-1.text: Two players share one measure. The top player plays two one-third notes. Build the bottom row from twelfths until it ends on the same beat. Press Play to check. How many twelfths did it take?

g3m-3-10-01-think-done.text: You heard it! Both rows ended on the same beat. Two-thirds and eight-twelfths fill the same amount. In the Lesson, you'll learn a word for this.

g3m-3-10-01-learn-1.text: Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn what equivalent fractions are. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own.

g3m-3-10-01-practice-1.text: Each job has a mix-up kids often make. A clue: the wholes must be the same size, and the parts must be equal. Then look at the length, not just the numbers.

g3m-3-10-01-own-1.text: Your turn to work on your own. Split every piece into two equal pieces. The shaded part stays the same length. Only its name changes.

g3m-3-10-01-swyk-1.text: Last stop! Show what you know. Fill one of Bach's measures any way you like. Then press Play and listen to your music.

g3m-3-10-01-end-1.text: Before you go, listen to Bach's music for a group of string players. Hear the long notes and quick notes fit together. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.

g3m-3-10-01-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us fractions that look different but fill the same amount. Watch the length.

g3m-3-10-01-vid-close.text: Same length, new name. That's what equivalent fractions are. Now it's your turn.

g3m-3-10-01-vid-math.text: Here is one measure of music. It is one whole. One whole note fills the whole measure. Cut it into two equal parts. Each part is one-half. Let's shade one half. Bach could play a half note here. Now cut every part in half again. There are four equal parts, and two are shaded. That's two-fourths. Two quarter notes take the same time as one half note. Cut every part in half one more time. Eight equal parts, and four are shaded. Four-eighths. Look at the shaded part. It never changed length. One-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths are the same amount. We call them equivalent fractions. Equivalent sounds like equal. They have the same value. Let's check on number lines. One line is in halves, one is in fourths, and one is in eighths. One-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths all land on the same spot. We can go the other way, too. This bar has ten equal parts, and two tenths are shaded. Group the tenths in pairs. Now there are five bigger parts, and one is shaded. Two-tenths is equal to one-fifth. Watch out! Every part must be split or grouped the same way, and the whole must stay the same size. Then the shaded amount stays the same.

g3m-3-10-02-vid-math.text: Here is one measure. It is one whole. Cut it in half and shade one part. One part is shaded, and there are two parts in all. One-half. Now split every part into two. Two parts are shaded, and there are four parts in all. Both counts doubled. One-half equals two-fourths. Go back to one-half, and split every part into three. Three are shaded, and there are six in all. Both counts are three times as many. One-half equals three-sixths. Split every part into four. Four shaded, eight in all. One-half equals four-eighths. Do you see the rule? Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number. We show it with arrows. Times four on the numerator. Times four on the denominator. The shaded part stays the same length, so the fraction is equivalent. Does it work for thirds, too? Here is two-thirds. Split every part into four. Eight are shaded, and there are twelve in all. Two times four is eight. Three times four is twelve. Two-thirds equals eight-twelfths. Watch out! Always multiply both numbers by the same number. If you change only one, the shaded part changes size.

g3m-3-10-03-vid-math.text: Here is a measure cut into ten parts. Eight are shaded. That's eight-tenths. Now group the parts in twos. Every two small parts make one bigger part. Count again. Four parts are shaded, and there are five in all. Eight divided by two is four. Ten divided by two is five. Eight-tenths equals four-fifths. Line up the two strips. The shaded parts are the same length. Here is sixteen-twentieths. Sofia divides both numbers by two, and gets eight-tenths. She divides by two again, and gets four-fifths. Small steps. Alex sees that four divides both numbers. Sixteen divided by four is four. Twenty divided by four is five. Four-fifths, in one big step. Both ways land in the same place. Can we divide four and five by the same number? Only by one. So four-fifths is in simplest form. It has the fewest, biggest parts. Watch out! Divide both numbers by the same number. If you divide only one number, or take away, the shaded part changes size.

g3m-3-10-04-vid-math.text: Here are four-fifths and seven-tenths. The bars are the same length, but the pieces are different sizes. So we can't just count yet. Let's re-cut. Cut each fifth into two pieces. Now both bars have tenths. Four-fifths is eight-tenths. Four times two is eight. Five times two is ten. Look, the shaded parts still line up. Re-cutting didn't change the amount. Eight-tenths is more than seven-tenths, so four-fifths is greater. That's Dion's way. He makes a common denominator. Emma has another way. Here are one-sixth and two-elevenths. She makes the numerators match. One-sixth is two-twelfths. Now both have two pieces. A twelfth is smaller than an eleventh. So two-elevenths is greater. That's a common numerator. Watch out! Don't compare only the numerators, or only the denominators. Re-cut first, so the pieces are the same size. Then compare.

g3m-3-10-04-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us two ways to compare fractions with different denominators. Watch the pieces.

g3m-3-10-04-vid-close.text: Same-size pieces make comparing fair. Re-cut, then count. Now it's your turn.

g3m-3-10-05-vid-math.text: Here are two-ninths and five-sevenths. Each cup is one whole. Let's draw a line at one-half. Half of nine is four and a half. Two-ninths is less than that, so it's less than one-half. Half of seven is three and a half. Five-sevenths is more than that, so it's more than one-half. So five-sevenths is greater. One-half is a benchmark. It's a number we compare to. Now here are nine-tenths and eleven-twelfths. Both are more than one-half, so the halfway line can't help. Look at the missing pieces instead. Each cup is missing one piece. A twelfth is smaller than a tenth. So eleven-twelfths is closer to full. Eleven-twelfths is greater. Watch out! Half of an odd number has a half in it. And the cup with the smaller missing piece is closer to one whole.

g3m-3-10-05-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us two shortcuts for comparing fractions. Watch the halfway line.

g3m-3-10-05-vid-close.text: Halfway line, or missing piece. Pick the shortcut that helps. Now it's your turn.

g3m-3-10-06-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to add and take away fractions. Watch the size of the pieces.

g3m-3-10-06-vid-close.text: Same-size pieces? Count them, and keep the unit. Now it's your turn.

g3m-3-10-06-vid-math.text: Four apples plus three apples is seven apples. Fractions work the same way. Here is one whole, cut into ninths. Four-ninths are shaded. Now add three more ninths. Count on: five, six, seven. Four-ninths plus three-ninths equals seven-ninths. Ninths are the unit. We counted ninths, so the answer is still in ninths. Now let's take some away. Start at seven-ninths on the number line. Take away five-ninths. Hop back five: six, five, four, three, two. We land on two-ninths. Seven-ninths minus five-ninths equals two-ninths. Watch out! Don't add the denominators. The pieces are still ninths, so the denominator stays nine. And to take away from one whole, cut it into pieces first. One whole is nine-ninths.

g3m-3-10-07-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us how clue words tell you what to do. Listen for them.

g3m-3-10-07-vid-close.text: Read the whole story, find the clue words, then do one step at a time. Now it's your turn!

g3m-3-10-07-vid-math.text: Read the whole story first. Here's one. Lena has two-elevenths of a meter of ribbon. She adds seven-elevenths more. Then she cuts off four-elevenths. Adds more means add. Two-elevenths plus seven-elevenths is nine-elevenths. Cuts off means take away. Nine-elevenths minus four-elevenths is five-elevenths. Do one step at a time, and keep elevenths the unit. Now a different clue. One candle is six-sevenths of a foot tall. The other is one-seventh of a foot. How much taller is the first candle? How much more, or how much taller, means find the gap. Line up the two bars. Count the extra pieces: one, two, three, four, five. The first candle is five-sevenths of a foot taller. We found the gap, so we took away. We did not add. Watch out! Check if your answer can be simpler. One-twelfth plus one-twelfth is two-twelfths. Two twelfths fit exactly under one sixth. So the simplest form is one-sixth.

g3m-3-10-07-words.text: Altogether. ... How much more. ... Clue word.

g3m-3-11-01-vid-math.text: This is a meter stick. It is one meter long. Look at the tiny spaces. Each one is one centimeter. Let's count them by tens. Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, one hundred. One meter is one hundred centimeters. Here's a rope. It is longer than one meter stick. Lay the meter stick at the end of the rope. That's one meter. Measure the rest with a centimeter ruler, starting at zero. It's forty-six centimeters. So the rope is one meter forty-six centimeters. In centimeters, that's one hundred plus forty-six, or one hundred forty-six centimeters. Now go the other way. A garden path is nine hundred thirty-five centimeters long. How many meters? Every hundred centimeters makes one meter. Nine hundreds make nine meters. Thirty-five centimeters are left over. So the path is nine meters thirty-five centimeters. Watch out! Eight meters three centimeters is not eighty-three centimeters. Eight meters is eight hundred centimeters. Add three more, and you get eight hundred three centimeters.

g3m-3-11-02-warm-1.text: Hoo! It's the day after we saw the marble meter. Now we're in a ribbon shop in Paris. The rolls of ribbon are measured in whole meters. But customers ask for pieces in centimeters. Look at the old picture of a busy Paris shop, full of ribbons and cloth. Today you'll cut pieces off whole meters and find out how much is left.

g3m-3-11-02-think-1.text: Here's the first order. The roll has nine whole meters. The customer wants forty-seven centimeters. You can't cut centimeters from a whole meter, so break one meter first.

g3m-3-11-02-think-done.text: Well done! You broke one meter into one hundred centimeters. You cut off forty-seven, and fifty-three were left. Eight whole meters are still on the roll. So eight meters fifty-three centimeters remain.

g3m-3-11-02-learn-1.text: Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows two ways to take centimeters away from meters. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you cut an order on your own.

g3m-3-11-02-practice-1.text: Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Break only one meter, and keep the other meters. Then check by adding back.

g3m-3-11-02-own-1.text: Your turn to work on your own. Take away the meters first. Then break a meter for the centimeters.

g3m-3-11-02-swyk-1.text: Last stop! The orders are coming in. Cut each one from the roll, and say what's left.

g3m-3-11-02-end-1.text: The shop is closing for the night. Listen to music by Joseph Haydn, first played in London in 1792. It's soft and quiet, and then, surprise, one big loud chord! Stories say he wanted to wake up sleepy listeners. Press play, and stop whenever you like.

g3m-3-11-02-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to take centimeters away from meters. Watch the meter break.

g3m-3-11-02-vid-math.text: A ribbon roll has nine meters. A customer wants twenty-eight centimeters. We can't take centimeters from a whole meter. So break one meter into one hundred centimeters. Now we have eight meters and one hundred centimeters. Take twenty-eight from the hundred. Count up from twenty-eight: two more makes thirty, and seventy more makes one hundred. Two and seventy is seventy-two. So seventy-two centimeters are left, and the eight meters are still there. Nine meters minus twenty-eight centimeters is eight meters seventy-two centimeters. Here's another way. Take away one whole meter. That leaves eight meters. But we only needed twenty-eight centimeters, so we took too much. Give back the extra seventy-two centimeters. Eight meters and seventy-two centimeters again. Watch out! Don't forget to break a meter. Nine meters minus twenty-eight centimeters is not nine meters seventy-two centimeters. One of the nine meters was broken, so only eight are left.

g3m-3-11-02-vid-close.text: Break one meter, keep the rest, and check by adding back. Now it's your turn!

g3m-3-11-02-words.text: Subtract. ... Remaining. ... Break a meter. ... Compound units.

g3m-3-11-03-warm-1.text: Hoo! It's Paris in the summer of 1793. On the highest hill in the city, Claude Chappe and his brothers built a wooden tower with arms that move. Each way the arms point stands for a signal. Far away, another tower watches through a telescope and copies the signal. Look at the old picture of their test. Today you'll measure long distances in kilometers and meters.

g3m-3-11-03-think-1.text: Before the test, a messenger runs a note from the workshop up to the tower. The path is one thousand nine hundred meters long. Build it out of hundred-meter pieces, and watch what happens at ten.

g3m-3-11-03-think-done.text: You did it! Ten pieces of one hundred meters made one kilometer. Nine more pieces made nine hundred meters. So one thousand nine hundred meters is one kilometer nine hundred meters.

g3m-3-11-03-learn-1.text: Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how meters build up to kilometers. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you work on your own.

g3m-3-11-03-practice-1.text: Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. A kilometer is one thousand meters, not one hundred. And always compare in the same unit.

g3m-3-11-03-own-1.text: Your turn to work on your own. Find the thousands first. Those are the kilometers.

g3m-3-11-03-swyk-1.text: Last stop! A message has to reach three stops along a road. Move it to each one, and say how far it went.

g3m-3-11-03-end-1.text: Here's music from about the same time as the towers. It's a slow part of a symphony by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, written in 1780. Listen to the strings, soft and smooth, like a signal passing from tower to tower. Press play, and stop whenever you like.

g3m-3-11-03-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us how meters add up to kilometers. Watch the road grow.

g3m-3-11-03-vid-math.text: Here is a road made of pieces. Each piece is one hundred meters long. Let's count by hundreds: one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, and so on, all the way to one thousand. Ten pieces of one hundred meters make one thousand meters. One thousand meters is one kilometer. A kilometer is about a fifteen-minute walk. Now let's build a longer road, three thousand four hundred meters long. Every ten pieces make a kilometer, so we have three kilometers. Four pieces are left over. That's four hundred meters. Three thousand four hundred meters is three kilometers four hundred meters. To go the other way, think of every kilometer as one thousand meters. Three kilometers four hundred meters is three thousand meters and four hundred meters, so three thousand four hundred meters. Watch out! A kilometer is not one hundred meters. Six kilometers is six thousand meters, not six hundred meters.

g3m-3-11-03-vid-close.text: Ten hundreds make a thousand, and a thousand meters make a kilometer. Now it's your turn!

g3m-3-11-03-words.text: Kilometer. ... Distance. ... Travel distance. ... Direct distance.

g3m-3-11-04-warm-1.text: Hoo! It's France in 1798. Jean-Baptiste Delambre and his team are measuring the land to find out how long a meter should be. Near the town of Melun, they measure a straight road almost twelve kilometers long. They lay metal rulers end to end, again and again. Look at an old picture of a team doing the same kind of job. Today you'll subtract meters from kilometers.

g3m-3-11-04-think-1.text: Today the team has three kilometers of road to measure. By lunch, they have measured four hundred fifty meters. How much road is left? Break a kilometer to find out.

g3m-3-11-04-think-done.text: You did it! You broke one kilometer into one thousand meters and cut off four hundred fifty. Five hundred fifty meters were left, plus two whole kilometers. So two kilometers five hundred fifty meters of road are left.

g3m-3-11-04-learn-1.text: Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to break a kilometer. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you work on your own.

g3m-3-11-04-practice-1.text: Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. A kilometer breaks into one thousand meters, not one hundred. And once you break it, that kilometer is gone.

g3m-3-11-04-own-1.text: Your turn to work on your own. Take away the whole kilometers first. Then break one kilometer for the meters.

g3m-3-11-04-swyk-1.text: Last stop! A road gets measured in two parts. Cut off each part, one after the other, and say how much road is left each time.

g3m-3-11-04-end-1.text: Here's music from the same years as the survey. It's the slow part of the London Symphony by Joseph Haydn, written in 1795. Listen to the calm, steady tune, like a team laying its rulers down a long, straight road. Press play, and stop whenever you like.

g3m-3-11-04-vid-open.text: Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to subtract meters from kilometers. Watch a kilometer break open.

g3m-3-11-04-vid-math.text: Here is a road six kilometers long. We need to take away one kilometer two hundred forty meters. First, take away the whole kilometer. Now five kilometers are left. Next, we need two hundred forty meters, but every piece here is a whole kilometer. So we break one kilometer. One kilometer is one thousand meters. Now we have four kilometers and one thousand meters. Cut off two hundred forty meters. One thousand minus two hundred forty is seven hundred sixty. So four kilometers seven hundred sixty meters are left. You can also use numbers. Six kilometers is six thousand meters. One kilometer two hundred forty meters is one thousand two hundred forty meters. Six thousand minus one thousand two hundred forty is four thousand seven hundred sixty meters. That's four kilometers seven hundred sixty meters, the same answer. Watch out! A broken kilometer is one thousand meters, not one hundred. And once you break it, that kilometer is gone. Count what's left in whole kilometers.

g3m-3-11-04-vid-close.text: Break a kilometer into one thousand meters, then take away. Now it's your turn!
